extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors, and news consumers interested in media ethics and newsroom practice
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and lessons for evaluating and producing newspaper journalism, with emphasis on editorial oversight, fact-checking, cognitive bias, and accountability in high-profile stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require reporters to reveal sources on sensitive stories
rubrics_metrics.description: “most notably requiring reporters to reveal their sources to editors on sensitive stories.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a post-mortem reform from the 'Jimmy' scandal: reporters should disclose sources to editors for sensitive investigations so editors can verify claims and assess credibility. This is presented as a concrete procedural change intended to prevent hoaxes and fabrications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic fact-checking / verify core facts
rubrics_metrics.description: The piece “fell apart in less than a full day of fact-checking. Virtually every aspect of the piece collapsed under the most basic scrutiny. Jimmy never existed, and no editor had ever bothered to see if he did.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors must verify the existence of central subjects and the basic factual claims of a story (names, locations, events). Failure to perform elementary checks (e.g., confirming whether a purported subject actually exists) is a critical anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look for and test disconfirming evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Top editors “could not see disconfirming evidence” because of a desire to believe the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters and editors should actively seek information that would contradict the narrative (devil’s-advocate checks). Treat storytelling plausibility as a hypothesis to be falsified rather than assumed true; failing to search for disconfirming facts enables hoaxes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for narrative red flags and implausibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of red flags: “Jimmy was remarkably eloquent for an 8-year-old... and the idea that adults would openly inject a child with heroin in front of a news reporter.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be suspicious of details that strain plausibility (unlikely dialogue, behavior, or scenarios). Use plausibility checks to trigger deeper verification rather than letting sensational detail stand on its own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hold ambition and desire for a big story in check
rubrics_metrics.description: “Editors and reporters are, by and large, an ambitious group. That ambition must held in check in search of accuracy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambition to publish dramatic, career-making pieces must not override verification processes. Editorial incentives and desires for prestige should be actively managed to avoid confirmation bias and rushed publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid institutional/prestige blind spots
rubrics_metrics.description: The failure was “not a lack of editorial oversight but rather the opposite: a burning desire by the top of the newspaper to believe” a reporter had broken a major story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Senior editors must not allow the institution’s recent successes, reputation, or excitement to reduce skepticism. High organizational confidence can create blind spots; leaders must enforce normal checks even (especially) when a scoop would reflect well on the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uphold rigid editorial standards
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is critically important that the newspaper upholds rigid editorial standards.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain clear, consistently enforced editorial policies and verification workflows. 'Rigid' here implies no exceptions for sensational stories—standards should apply uniformly to protect credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance speed/impact with accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: In the “frenzied rush to continue the paper’s upward trajectory” editors overlooked disconfirming evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid letting competitive or commercial pressures for quick, attention-grabbing content trump the need for thorough verification. Prioritize accuracy over speed when stakes are high.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize high stakes of erroneous reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Erroneous print reporting has led to major national harms (e.g., Vietnam escalation,Anthrax misreports, search for nonexistent WMDs, misreporting around drug epidemics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand and weigh the public-policy and societal consequences of publishing errors; the potential harm should increase the rigor of checks and editorial caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors must ruthlessly and constantly reflect on cognitive biases
rubrics_metrics.description: “Editors must ruthlessly and constantly reflect on their own cognitive biases.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make bias-awareness an explicit part of editorial practice: training, checklists, pre-publication reviews for motivated reasoning, and institutional mechanisms that require dissenting assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hold reporters and editors publicly accountable
rubrics_metrics.description: “We, as consumers of their product, hold editors and reporters to account.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accountability mechanisms (public corrections, retractions, institutional review, sanctions) and reader oversight are important to maintain trust. Encourage transparency about errors and corrective steps taken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fulfill journalism’s public-interest mission
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers “underpin American society by holding the powerful to account” and should “afflict the comfortable and comfort the afflicted.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate reporting by whether it serves the public interest and holds power to account; stories should illuminate truthfully rather than merely sensationalize. This mission justifies rigorous standards and ethical responsibility.
